ProME splits prototype margins at their median to construct approximately balanced environments along the training trajectory, and fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank the resulting predictors by validation worst-group accuracy. We theoretically bound the worst risk across the inferred environments for a fixed predictor and partition, showing that this bound transfers to the oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition. Extensive experiments show that prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation, and ProME achieves the highest average worst-group accuracy among the compared methods with the same group-label access.

AI.tldr: ProME is a new method for group-robust learning without training-group labels that aligns environment inference and representation selection with the deployed predictor, using prototype margins to construct balanced environments and achieving state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing group-robust learning methods often fail when training-group labels are unavailable. Current approaches infer environments from separate reference models and select representations before fitting the final classifier, causing misalignment with the deployed predictor.
AI.method: ProME formulates group robustness as the ERAS (endogenous environments with repair-aware selection) problem. It uses prototype margins (splitting at median) to construct approximately balanced environments along the training trajectory, then fits a group-balanced linear head on validation data to rank predictors by worst-group accuracy.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows worst risk bound across inferred environments transfers to oracle groups under alignment conditions. Experiments demonstrate prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation, and ProME achieves highest average worst-group accuracy among comparable methods with same group-label access.
AI.conclusion: ProME successfully addresses the misalignment problem in group-robust learning without training-group labels by jointly optimizing environment inference and predictor selection, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements in worst-group accuracy.

title: vToken: Token-Level Virtualization for Reclaimable KV Caches
summary: Large language model serving faces a critical memory bottleneck: the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention uses fixed-size memory blocks to reduce allocator-level fragmentation, but recent KV eviction algorithms operate at a token granularity finer than block-level management. This mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable. We present vToken, a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. vToken maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and realizes physical reclamation by repacking live tokens asynchronously. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility. We implement vToken in vLLM and evaluate it with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models. Compared with a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2\%--72.3\% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37$\times$. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends the maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2$\times$, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.

AI.tldr: vToken introduces token-level virtualization to solve intra-block fragmentation in KV cache management, enabling more efficient memory reclamation while maintaining compatibility with existing systems.
AI.motivation: Large language model serving faces memory bottlenecks from KV cache growth. While PagedAttention reduces allocator fragmentation, current KV eviction algorithms operate at token-level, causing intra-block fragmentation where allocated KV memory becomes unreclaimable.
AI.method: vToken implements a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. It maintains stable logical token views through token-table indirection and performs asynchronous repacking of live tokens for physical reclamation.
AI.result: vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2%-72.3%, improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37×, extends maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2× under constrained active-KV budget, and reduces integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.
AI.conclusion: vToken effectively solves intra-block fragmentation in KV cache management, enabling more efficient memory utilization while maintaining compatibility with existing PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph systems.

title: Beyond Simulated Benchmarks: Evaluating Motion Representations for Fall Detection Under Real-World Data Scarcity
summary: Falls are a major health concern for older adults, and wearable sensors have been widely explored for detecting falls and enabling timely intervention. However, real-world falls are extremely rare: collecting 100 of them requires an estimated 100,000 days of monitoring, resulting in severely limited labelled data for training machine learning models. Consequently, many approaches rely on simulated datasets, often reporting high laboratory performance but limited real-world generalisation. We present a systematic evaluation of motion representations for wearable fall detection under real-world data scarcity. Using accelerometer signals, we compare interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model representations. As an interpretable baseline, we additionally investigate a lightweight symbolic representation that converts short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Experiments use FallAllD, a simulated falls dataset, and FARSEEING, a clinically verified real-world falls dataset. Through cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer, we examine how representation choices affect robustness under realistic deployment. Our results reveal that highly parameterised kernel and foundation models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under both data scarcity and domain shift. Although the interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance, augmenting a symbolic representation with physically-grounded impact descriptors yields the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity, albeit at lower precision. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating beyond simulated benchmarks and show that representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given the scarcity of real-world data.

AI.tldr: Comparing motion representations for wearable fall detection under real-world data scarcity shows that simple interpretable models with physically-grounded features maintain robustness better than complex models when facing domain shift and limited data.
AI.motivation: Falls are a major health concern for older adults, but real-world falls are extremely rare (estimated 100 falls require 100,000 monitoring days), creating severe data scarcity. Many approaches use simulated datasets with high lab performance but poor real-world generalization, highlighting the need for robust representations that work under realistic data constraints.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of four motion representations using accelerometer signals: interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model representations. Also investigated a lightweight symbolic representation augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Experiments used FallAllD (simulated falls) and FARSEEING (clinically verified real-world falls) datasets with cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer analysis.
AI.result: Highly parameterized kernel and foundation models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under both data scarcity and domain shift. Interval-based representation achieves strongest absolute real-world performance. Augmented symbolic representation with physically-grounded impact descriptors yields smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity (albeit with lower precision).
AI.conclusion: Representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given real-world data scarcity. Simple interpretable models with physically-grounded features maintain robustness better than complex models when facing domain shift. Research should evaluate beyond simulated benchmarks and consider representation robustness under realistic deployment constraints.

title: Sovereign by necessity? Frontier AI export controls, cyber security, and the limits of national AI capability
summary: A small number of firms based in two states produce the most capable frontier AI models. The governments of those states have shown both the legal power and the political will to decide which other countries may use these systems. In June 2026 the United States required a leading developer to obtain licences before releasing its most advanced models to any foreign person, including foreign nationals resident in the United States. The affected models were withdrawn worldwide at short notice, partly because the restriction proved impractical to administer. This followed within months of the first documented case of a largely autonomous, AI-run cyber espionage campaign, and coincided with mounting evidence that frontier models alter the economics of both cyber attack and cyber defence. This article examines how these two developments interact, and situates them within the unusual market dynamics now driving large-scale AI development. It argues that access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defence, that such access can be revoked, and that the obvious remedy of sovereign capability remains only partly feasible for all but a handful of states. Drawing on evidence about training costs, the concentration of computing power and the support offered by national AI programmes, it asks what sovereignty can realistically mean for small and middle powers, and for large powers as well. The article proposes a layered strategy: negotiated access guarantees, sovereignty at the level of inference, hedging with open-weight models, pooled regional capability, sustained talent development and continued investment in basic cyber resilience. The open-weight hedge proves at once more capable and more politically exposed than is commonly assumed. Much of the near-term risk lies in how capable models are deployed and contained rather than in their apparent performance.

AI.tldr: Frontier AI access is becoming a national cyber defense resource, but this access is controlled by only a few countries and can be revoked, creating sovereignty challenges for most nations.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from two key developments: 1) US restrictions on exporting advanced AI models in June 2026, showing that AI access can be controlled by powerful states, and 2) The first documented autonomous AI-run cyber espionage campaign, demonstrating that frontier models change cyber attack/defense economics.
AI.method: The article examines the interaction between these developments and situates them within the unusual market dynamics driving large-scale AI development. It analyzes evidence about training costs, computing power concentration, and national AI programs to assess realistic sovereignty options.
AI.result: Access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defense, but this access is controlled by only a few states and can be revoked. Sovereign AI capability remains feasible for only a handful of states due to high costs and resource concentration. Open-weight models, while promising, are more politically exposed than commonly assumed.
AI.conclusion: The article proposes a layered strategy including negotiated access guarantees, sovereignty at inference level, hedging with open-weight models, regional capability pooling, talent development, and cyber resilience investment. Near-term risk depends more on deployment and containment than model performance.

title: TANGCO: Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures
summary: Networked systems, from power grids to traffic networks and cloud clusters, carry loads across nodes with limited capacity. A node whose load exceeds its capacity fails and sheds its load onto its neighbors, which can trigger a system-wide cascade. We study how to allocate a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist these cascades under local load redistribution. The problem is difficult because no optimal allocation is known, and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, so exact and gradient-based optimization methods do not directly apply. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which uses a graph neural network policy trained through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor. We evaluate TANGCO on five synthetic graph families and five real networks spanning power, road, air, and Internet topologies. The learned policy improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%. The learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies, and TANGCO$^{pre}$, pre-trained on synthetic graphs, matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO$^{pre}$ allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic. Free-vector variants without the GNN, stay close to the heuristics, so the graph representation carries the gain beyond numerical search. Finally, analysis of the learned allocations identifies when local risk is sufficient, leads to an improved closed-form heuristic, and reveals the regimes where a topology-aware learned policy remains necessary.

AI.tldr: TANGCO uses graph neural networks trained with policy gradients to optimize capacity allocation for cascade resilience in networked systems, outperforming hand-designed heuristics across diverse networks.
AI.motivation: Networked systems have nodes with limited capacity to handle loads; when overloaded, nodes fail and redistribute load to neighbors, potentially triggering system-wide cascades. Existing optimization approaches struggle because the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, and no optimal allocation is known.
AI.method: TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization) uses a graph neural network policy trained through a cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor. The approach involves: 1) Training GNN policies through interaction with cascade simulators, 2) Using policy-gradient optimization for the non-differentiable objective, 3) Incorporating heuristic anchors, and 4) Evaluating on both synthetic and real networks.
AI.result: The learned policy outperforms the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%. The method shows transfer learning capabilities across graphs within families, pre-training on synthetic graphs matches per-network training on real networks, and scales near-linearly with graph size.
AI.conclusion: TANGCO provides an effective data-driven approach for cascade-resistant capacity allocation that significantly outperforms traditional heuristics. The GNN representation is crucial for the performance gains, and analysis of learned allocations reveals when local risk assessment suffices versus when topology-aware learned policies remain necessary. The method offers practical deployment advantages with pre-training matching hand-designed heuristic costs.

title: Towards Context-Aware Clinical Motion Understanding in Daily Living at Home: Freezing of Gait Detection with Egocentric Vision
comment: Accepted to ECCV Workshop 2026 (Human Motion Challenges in Real-World and Clinical Settings)
summary: Understanding motion in daily living requires context beyond kinematics, because similar inertial patterns during activities of daily living (ADLs) can reflect intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological movement impairment. Egocentric vision provides task-related context that may help disambiguate these cases. We investigate this challenge through freezing of gait (FOG) detection in Parkinson's disease (PD), a symptom strongly influenced by contextual factors during ADLs. Using synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels collected from 13 PD participants in their homes, we evaluate frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, alongside an IMU-based TCN trained from scratch, under leave-one-subject-out evaluation. The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest event-detection performance, reaching 42.3 F1 and 83.0 AUROC, compared with 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC for V-JEPA2 ego-video features. Although ego-video alone did not outperform IMU-based sensing, it showed above-chance discrimination, and qualitative analyses suggest that egocentric vision may capture FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs. Together, these results support the use of pretrained ego-video representations to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using egocentric video alongside IMU sensors to improve freezing of gait detection in Parkinson's disease patients, finding that while IMU-based methods perform best, ego-video adds valuable contextual information.
AI.motivation: Understanding motion in daily living requires more than just kinematic data, as similar inertial patterns can result from different causes (intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological impairment). Egocentric vision provides task-related context that could help disambiguate these cases, particularly for freezing of gait detection in Parkinson's disease which is strongly influenced by contextual factors during activities of daily living.
AI.method: The study used synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels collected from 13 Parkinson's disease participants in their homes. Researchers evaluated frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, alongside an IMU-based Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) trained from scratch, using leave-one-subject-out evaluation.
AI.result: The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest performance with 42.3 F1 score and 83.0 AUROC. V-JEPA2 ego-video features performed less well with 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC. While ego-video alone didn't outperform IMU sensing, it showed above-chance discrimination, and qualitative analyses suggest egocentric vision captures FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs.
AI.conclusion: The results support using pretrained ego-video representations to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living, suggesting a complementary role for vision alongside inertial sensing for improved clinical assessment.

title: History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision (PRCV 2026) as an oral paper
summary: Forecasting the long-horizon evolution of mechanical systems from position-only observations is a pivotal yet difficult task, as hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical properties must be inferred simultaneously. Although physics-guided neural networks like Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) guarantee physical plausibility, they generally require complete state inputs and lack adaptability to changing system parameters. To break these limitations, we introduce History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks (HiLNN). Grounded in the insight that temporal position sequences implicitly encode underlying dynamics, HiLNN employs a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from history. This context not only reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity but also adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. By leveraging a differentiable RK4 rollout scheme, the entire pipeline is optimized end-to-end under multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization. Empirical evaluations across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems show that HiLNN delivers superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yingtian22/History-informed-LNN.

AI.tldr: HiLNN uses a recurrent encoder to extract latent context from position-only history, enabling simultaneous velocity reconstruction and adaptive physics parameter learning for accurate long-term mechanical system forecasting.
AI.motivation: Traditional physics-guided neural networks like Lagrangian Neural Networks require complete state inputs (positions and velocities) and lack adaptability to changing system parameters, limiting their practical application for forecasting mechanical systems from position-only observations.
AI.method: HiLNN employs a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from historical position sequences, which simultaneously reconstructs unobserved initial velocities and adaptively modulates mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients. It uses differentiable RK4 rollout with multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization for end-to-end optimization.
AI.result: HiLNN achieves superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks effectively address the limitations of traditional physics-guided approaches by enabling position-only forecasting with adaptive physical parameter learning, making them suitable for real-world mechanical system prediction where velocities are unobserved and parameters vary.

title: NAS-Driven Hardware Accelerator Exploration for Edge AI and Quantization Effects on the Pareto Space
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, accepted for presentation to the 39th IEEE International System-on-Chip Conference, Heidelberg, Germany, September 30 - October 2, 2026
summary: Edge AI deployment demands neural architectures that are simultaneously accurate, computationally efficient, and hardware-deployable - a challenge addressed by hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS). While recent works incorporate quantization directly into the NAS loop, these approaches expand search complexity and tightly couple architecture and quantization design. The simpler post-search quantization strategy has received little analytical attention: the effects of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) on the NAS-discovered Pareto structure remain uncharacterised, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration. This paper addresses both gaps. First, a three-stage pipeline is proposed: a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. Second, an empirical study characterises how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space through formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures, and demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-stage pipeline for Edge AI deployment that bridges neural architecture search with post-training quantization and hardware mapping, while empirically studying how quantization affects NAS Pareto spaces.
AI.motivation: Edge AI requires neural architectures that are accurate, computationally efficient, and hardware-deployable. Existing approaches either expand search complexity by incorporating quantization into NAS or use simpler post-search quantization without proper analysis of its effects on NAS Pareto structures. There's also no framework combining quantized architecture mapping with automated hardware exploration for reconfigurable accelerators.
AI.method: Proposes a three-stage pipeline: 1) hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, 2) quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and 3) evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. Also conducts empirical study analyzing how INT4 Post-Training Quantization perturbs NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space using formal stability metrics on all 15,625 architectures.
AI.result: Demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies. The framework successfully bridges NAS with quantization and hardware mapping while characterizing quantization effects on architecture search.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework addresses key gaps in Edge AI deployment by providing an integrated approach for hardware-aware NAS with quantization analysis and automated hardware exploration, showing that simpler post-search quantization strategies with proper analysis can be effective for Edge AI deployment on reconfigurable accelerators.

title: Knowledge-guided Pattern Discovery via Coupled Tensor Factorizations
summary: In order to understand complex systems such as the human metabolome or human brain, different sensing technologies are used, generating complex data. These datasets are often multiway, i.e., with more than two axes of variation such as a subjects by metabolites by time array. While tensor factorizations have successfully revealed interpretable patterns from such complex data, they have so far been mainly data-driven. On the other hand, there is more to data -- there are computational models (of these systems), which are rich sources of prior information. In this paper, we introduce a knowledge-guided approach that brings together data and computational models by jointly analyzing real data and simulated data (generated using a computational model) using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling. Our experiments on real metabolomics measurements demonstrate that guiding the analysis of such noisy data with simulated data improves the pattern discovery performance while also revealing potential discrepancies between data and computational models.

AI.tldr: A knowledge-guided tensor factorization approach that jointly analyzes real and simulated data using linear coupling to improve pattern discovery in complex systems like metabolomics.
AI.motivation: Current tensor factorization methods for analyzing multiway data (like metabolomics) are mainly data-driven and don't incorporate existing computational models that contain valuable prior information about complex biological systems.
AI.method: Introduces a knowledge-guided approach using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling to jointly analyze real data and simulated data generated from computational models.
AI.result: Experiments on real metabolomics measurements show that guiding analysis with simulated data improves pattern discovery performance and can reveal potential discrepancies between data and computational models.
AI.conclusion: Combining data-driven tensor factorizations with computational model simulations through linear coupling enhances pattern discovery in complex biological systems while providing insights into model-data consistency.

title: StateBridge: Training-free Hidden-state Alignment for Latent Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, accepted by COLM2026
summary: Large language model based multi-agent systems usually communicate in text, i.e., using discrete tokens. However, text introduces a discrete bottleneck. Converting the sender's continuous hidden states into discrete tokens discards information that token identities alone cannot capture. Recent work proposes latent communication as an alternative, where agents transmit hidden representations directly without converting them to text. However, existing latent methods either inject working memory layer by layer across the transformers, or require trained projectors that limit portability. We propose StateBridge, a training-free latent communication approach that aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transformation. Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring ensure compatibility with the pretrained input distribution. The aligned states are prepended to the input of the receiver agent as a continuous prefix. We evaluate StateBridge on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering with four models from two families. StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: StateBridge is a training-free latent communication method for multi-agent LLMs that uses orthogonal transformation to align sender hidden states to receiver input space, avoiding discrete text bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Text-based communication between LLM agents creates a discrete bottleneck, discarding valuable continuous information from hidden states. Existing latent communication methods either inject memory across transformer layers or require trained projectors that limit portability.
AI.method: StateBridge aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space using a closed-form orthogonal transformation. It includes lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring for compatibility. The aligned states are prepended to the receiver's input as a continuous prefix.
AI.result: StateBridge achieves best or tied-best scores on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs across math reasoning, code generation, and question answering with four models from two families, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: StateBridge provides an effective, training-free solution for latent communication between LLM agents that avoids discrete text bottlenecks, demonstrating superior performance across diverse tasks and model families without requiring complex training.

title: Novel Knowledge-Guided Generative Methods for Synthetic Transcriptomic Data
summary: As biomedical research increasingly relies on data-intensive tools, the quality and utility of datasets are critical. Challenges such as imbalances, biases, and ethical or legal constraints often limit access to high-quality data. Synthetic data generation can help overcome these limitations. Here, we present a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, investigating strategies to incorporate prior biological knowledge via gene graphs. This ensures that synthetic data capture real-world gene patterns, maintaining their usefulness for downstream tasks. In particular, we introduce and benchmark three variants of the Generative Adversarial Network. Among the alternatives, MK-TGAN - an innovative multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based model - stands out for its performance in terms of both the realism and utility of the generated data. Unlike other methods, MK-TGAN leverages prior knowledge graphs by exploiting graph neural networks. Our results show that prior knowledge integration strategies improve performance, and that MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, introducing MK-TGAN - a multi-kernel GNN-based model that outperforms alternatives by effectively incorporating biological knowledge graphs to generate realistic and useful synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Biomedical research faces challenges with data quality and accessibility due to imbalances, biases, and ethical/legal constraints. Synthetic data generation can help overcome these limitations, especially for transcriptomic data where preserving biological patterns is crucial.
AI.method: The researchers compare generative models for transcriptomic data, focusing on strategies to incorporate prior biological knowledge via gene graphs. They introduce and benchmark three GAN variants, with MK-TGAN being their main innovation - a multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based model that leverages knowledge graphs through GNNs.
AI.result: MK-TGAN outperforms alternative methods in terms of both realism and utility of generated synthetic data. Results show that prior knowledge integration strategies improve performance, and MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility.
AI.conclusion: Integration of prior biological knowledge via gene graphs improves synthetic data generation for transcriptomics. MK-TGAN, with its multi-kernel GNN architecture, represents an effective approach that produces high-quality, biologically plausible synthetic data for downstream biomedical applications.

title: LLM-Guided Graph Generation for Structure-Based Local Improvement Methods
summary: Large neighborhood search normally selects a random subset of decision variables for iterative optimization. For efficiently solving different problems, researchers tend to design variable selection strategies by taking into account structural features from different domains. In this paper, we build an automatic pipeline that is problem-agnostic to all problems in the MiniZinc format. By prompting an LLM with our semantic guidelines, we guide the LLM to produce a graph generator that maps any instance of a problem type to a uniform weighted graph, where nodes represent decision variables and edges represent constraint relationships. These problem-agnostic graphs guide our structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) in variable selection. Meanwhile, the weighted graph enables all problem instances to share the same generic graph representation, from which the same graph features can be extracted and used for configuration selection. We evaluated our pipeline on instances across 20 MiniZinc competition problems, finding that algorithm selection achieves a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation boost the performance further to 44.0%, demonstrating that LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure extraction and feature extraction for constraint optimization.

AI.tldr: LLM-based pipeline generates problem-agnostic graph representations from MiniZinc problems, enabling automatic structure extraction for improved variable selection in constraint optimization.
AI.motivation: Traditional large neighborhood search requires domain-specific variable selection strategies. The paper aims to create a problem-agnostic approach that can automatically extract structural features from any MiniZinc problem without manual domain expertise.
AI.method: 1) Use LLM prompting with semantic guidelines to generate a graph generator; 2) Map any problem instance to uniform weighted graphs (nodes = variables, edges = constraints); 3) Use these graphs in Structure-based Local Improvement Framework (SLIM) for variable selection; 4) Extract graph features for configuration selection across all problems.
AI.result: Tested on 20 MiniZinc competition problems: algorithm selection achieved 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against Gurobi baseline (vs. 19.3% best single configuration). With configuration and feature ablation, performance improved to 44.0%, demonstrating effective automated structure extraction.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based semantic generation enables automatic structure and feature extraction for constraint optimization, achieving significantly better performance than domain-specific approaches while being problem-agnostic.

title: Virtual Temperature Sensors in Power Transformers Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
summary: Accurate modeling and forecasting of power transformer thermal behavior are critical for reliability, asset lifetime, and optimized power system operation. Numerical approaches such as finite element methods (FEM) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) offer high fidelity but are computationally expensive, require complex mesh generation, and are often impractical for real-time or large-scale applications, particularly when transformer geometries are unknown. Lumped-parameter thermal models are more practical but depend on transformer-specific thermal constants and may fail to capture dynamic responses under varying operating and environmental conditions. Purely data-driven machine learning methods, including artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown success in forecasting transformer temperatures but typically require large volumes of high-quality training data and may produce physically inconsistent or uninterpretable results. This paper develops a physics-aware Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework for forecasting transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data. Neural ODEs model system dynamics in continuous time, providing smooth trajectory prediction and a natural representation of continuously evolving thermal dynamics. A key contribution is the integration of simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation. The model is evaluated across datasets from fifteen transformers in different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms. The results demonstrate that the developed Neural ODE framework provides a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting approach for heterogeneous transformer units.

AI.tldr: Physics-aware Neural ODE framework for forecasting power transformer thermal behavior that integrates simplified heat-transfer equations into continuous-time modeling, providing accurate and physically consistent predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches have limitations: FEM/CFD methods are computationally expensive and require complex geometry knowledge; lumped-parameter models lack accuracy under varying conditions; purely data-driven ML methods require large datasets and produce uninterpretable results. Need for a standardized, physics-aware approach for heterogeneous transformers.
AI.method: Develops a physics-aware Neural ODE (Neural Ordinary Differential Equation) framework that models thermal dynamics in continuous time. Integrates simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation, combining data-driven learning with physical principles.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15 transformers from different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms. The framework provides standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting for heterogeneous transformer units, demonstrating improved performance over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The physics-aware Neural ODE framework offers a practical solution for transformer thermal forecasting that balances computational efficiency with physical consistency, providing accurate predictions across diverse transformer types without requiring extensive training data or detailed geometry knowledge.

title: LongEarth-R1: Benchmarking and Aligning Vision-Language Models for Long-Horizon Earth Observation Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon Earth observation reasoning requires models to organize multi-stage geographic evolution, localize spatial changes, detect temporal anomalies, and infer future from extended image sequences. However, existing remote sensing vision-language models mainly focus on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, limiting reliable grounding in the relevant frames and regions. We introduce LongEarth-Bench, a benchmark containing approximately 120k question-answering samples derived from 117k unique images. Its sequences average 15.14 frames and extend to 30 frames, covering 12 tasks across evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction. A 30k-sample subset further provides structured reasoning traces linking key frames and changed regions to final answers. We develop LongEarth through supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. Building on LongEarth, LongEarth-R1 applies group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards. LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: LongEarth is a new benchmark and model for long-horizon Earth observation reasoning that handles extended image sequences (up to 30 frames) across 12 tasks, with structured reasoning and reinforcement learning improvements.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing vision-language models focus only on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, which limits their ability to reliably ground reasoning in relevant frames and regions for long-horizon Earth observation tasks requiring multi-stage geographic evolution analysis.
AI.method: Created LongEarth-Bench with 120k QA samples from 117k unique images (average 15.14 frames, up to 30 frames). Developed LongEarth model through supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. Then created LongEarth-R1 using group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards.
AI.result: LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks in the LongEarth-Bench benchmark while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a comprehensive solution for long-horizon Earth observation reasoning, addressing limitations of existing models through a large-scale benchmark, structured reasoning supervision, and reinforcement learning optimization, enabling better analysis of extended temporal sequences in remote sensing.

title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have advanced primarily through architectural innovation, while training regimes for large-scale heterogeneous corpora remain under-explored. As a result, pre-training distributions are often poorly controlled with respect to domain imbalance, context requirements, prediction horizons, and missingness. We introduce ORBIT (Omni-Range Bootstrap Incremental Training), a training paradigm that makes this distribution explicit and controllable. ORBIT combines Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling, which controls dataset exposure and samples records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons, with Omni-Range Incremental Training, which varies context lengths and prediction horizons throughout a single training stage. Under ORBIT, we train Falcon-2.0, a simple univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction. We further introduce Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment, a training objective that uses late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers without additional inference cost. Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.

AI.tldr: TSFMs lack controlled training; ORBIT enables explicit distribution control via bootstrap sampling and incremental training, used to train Falcon-2.0 with novel architecture and training objectives, achieving strong zero-shot forecasting performance.
AI.motivation: Time series foundation models have advanced mainly through architectural innovation, but training regimes for large-scale heterogeneous corpora remain under-explored. Current pre-training distributions are poorly controlled with respect to domain imbalance, context requirements, prediction horizons, and missingness.
AI.method: Introduces ORBIT (Omni-Range Bootstrap Incremental Training) with two components: 1) Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling to control dataset exposure and sample records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons, and 2) Omni-Range Incremental Training to vary context lengths and prediction horizons within a single training stage. Also presents Falcon-2.0 architecture (univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction) and Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment objective (using late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers).
AI.result: Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.
AI.conclusion: ORBIT provides a controllable training paradigm for TSFMs that addresses distribution control challenges, enabling effective training of models like Falcon-2.0 that achieve competitive zero-shot forecasting capabilities across varied time series domains.

title: Rules or Character? Scaling Laws for AI Safety Design
comment: Accepted at AIES 2026 (9th AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society). 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) safety systems combine character shaping (e.g., Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback [RLHF], Constitutional AI), which modifies behavioral distributions at training time, with rule enforcement (e.g., output filters, safety classifiers), which blocks harmful outputs at inference time, yet little formal analysis exists on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scales increase. We introduce a stylized comparative-statics model that parameterizes safety design as a resource allocation alpha in [0,1] between these two approaches, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility -- the risk that shaped behavior degrades or collapses under novel conditions. Under a multiplicative Pareto damage model, we derive closed-form expected harm and supplement it with tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation. Across three scenarios (optimistic, moderate, pessimistic), the optimal alpha* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows, from negligible (Delta alpha* = +0.01) to pronounced (Delta alpha* = +0.21) depending on scenario. The dominant parameter is the baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag, which shifts alpha* by 0.50 across its range -- far exceeding the effect of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T. These results suggest that safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a mathematical model showing that optimal AI safety design depends more on character shaping reliability under distributional shift than on deployment scale, with character fragility being the dominant parameter.
AI.motivation: AI safety systems combine character shaping (training-time modification) with rule enforcement (inference-time blocking), but there's little formal analysis on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scales increase.
AI.method: A stylized comparative-statics model parameterizes safety design as resource allocation between character shaping and rule enforcement, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility. Uses multiplicative Pareto damage model with closed-form expected harm and CVaR analysis via Monte Carlo simulation.
AI.result: Optimal allocation is interior or at rules-only boundary, shifting weakly toward character shaping as scale grows (Δα* = +0.01 to +0.21). Character fragility rate is dominant parameter (shifts α* by 0.50), exceeding effects of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large scale.
AI.conclusion: Safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale than on character shaping reliability under distributional shift, with character fragility being the most important consideration for optimal safety design.

title: EEG Decoding Using CNN and LSTM Network
summary: Motor imagery (MI) brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a promising approach for establishing flexible communication pathways between the human brain and external devices , particularly for individuals affected by stroke or neurodegenerative disorders. Reliable decoding of motor-imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) remains challenging because EEG recordings contain substantial noise and exhibit complex, weakly informative relationships with the underlying brain activity. Although deep learning provides an effective means of learning representations directly from EEG signals, its application to MI-EEG feature learning remains comparatively limited. This study introduces a hybrid deep-learning architecture that integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a bidirectional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) network. The CNN is used to learn high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG recordings, whereas the bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies and relationships among the extracted features. The proposed approach is evaluated using both a publicly available dataset and a privately acquired dataset obtained with an EEG acquisition system. The experimental results indicate that the CNN\&bi-LSTM architecture provides robust performance for both two- and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability across the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: A hybrid CNN+bi-LSTM architecture for motor imagery EEG classification that learns spatial-temporal features from raw EEG signals, achieving robust performance on both public and private datasets with promising subject-independent decoding capability.
AI.motivation: MI-BCIs are promising for brain-device communication in stroke/neurodegenerative patients, but reliable MI-EEG decoding is challenging due to substantial noise and weak informative relationships in EEG signals. While deep learning can learn representations directly from EEG, its application to MI-EEG feature learning remains limited.
AI.method: Proposed a hybrid deep-learning architecture combining CNN with bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM). CNN learns high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG recordings, while bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies and relationships among extracted features.
AI.result: The CNN+bi-LSTM architecture demonstrates robust performance for both two- and three-class motor-imagery classification. Shows promising subject-independent decoding capability across evaluated methods on both publicly available dataset and privately acquired EEG dataset.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid CNN+bi-LSTM architecture effectively addresses MI-EEG decoding challenges by learning discriminative spatial-temporal features from raw signals, showing robust classification performance and potential for subject-independent applications in BCI systems.

title: TopoIntent: Compiling Security Intent into Executable, Compliance-Checked Network Topologies
summary: Enterprise security topology design requires translating business intent, regulatory requirements, and risk assumptions into zones, boundary devices, inter-zone paths, and access-control policies. Existing NetOps automation tools mainly operate after this design is fixed, providing limited support for generating structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. We present TopoIntent, a system that compiles security intent into executable, compliance-checked network topologies. It uses a schema contract to constrain generation, retrieves reference architectures from a curated template library via dense-vector search, and applies staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion. The generated topology is checked against CIS Controls v8.1.2 safeguards visible at the topology layer, while unresolved cases are marked for manual review. Structural gaps are repaired through additive schema-preserving edits. The final topology is exported to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs, enabling executable reachability and allow/deny tests. Because no public benchmark exists for this requirement-to-topology task, we construct an evaluation set from reference security architecture diagrams. The retrieval set contains 22 templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, while the held-out set contains 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios excluded from retrieval. On the held-out set, additive repair improves topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raises the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88.

AI.tldr: TopoIntent is a system that automatically generates compliant network security topologies from natural-language security requirements using template retrieval and staged fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing NetOps tools mainly operate after security design is fixed, providing limited support for generating structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. There's a gap in automating the translation of business intent, regulatory requirements, and risk assumptions into executable network topologies.
AI.method: Uses a schema contract to constrain generation, retrieves reference architectures from a curated template library via dense-vector search, applies staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion, performs CIS Controls v8.1.2 compliance checking, and repairs structural gaps through additive schema-preserving edits.
AI.result: On held-out evaluation set, additive repair improves topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raises post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88. The system generates executable Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs.
AI.conclusion: TopoIntent demonstrates effective automation of security topology generation from natural-language requirements, achieving high compliance rates and showing promise for reducing manual design effort while maintaining security standards.

title: Large-scale Testing Global Optimization Methods with Black-box Adversarial Attacks
summary: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are of a moderate size and are based on a small number of analytical functions that date back even to the 1970s. This causes a risk of biasing the development of global optimization methods. We argue that the tasks related to the black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) can serve as valuable global optimization benchmark in many-dimensional space. We demonstrate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics in solving example BBAA problems. Thus, we take a step towards convergence of global optimization methods to the challenges and needs that arise in the modern machine learning field.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using black-box adversarial attack tasks as modern global optimization benchmarks to replace outdated analytical functions, demonstrating evolutionary algorithms' effectiveness on these problems.
AI.motivation: The paper argues that existing global optimization benchmarks are outdated, moderately sized, and based on old analytical functions from the 1970s. This creates a risk of bias in developing new optimization methods that don't reflect modern challenges in fields like machine learning.
AI.method: The authors propose using black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) tasks as new global optimization benchmarks in many-dimensional space. They demonstrate and evaluate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics in solving example BBAA problems.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics are effective at solving black-box adversarial attack problems. This provides evidence that BBAA tasks can serve as valuable global optimization benchmarks that better reflect modern computational challenges.
AI.conclusion: Black-box adversarial attack tasks can serve as valuable and modern global optimization benchmarks, helping to align optimization method development with current challenges in machine learning and other fields, while evolutionary algorithms show promise in solving these problems.

title: Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model
summary: Existing predictive models in learning analytics often treat student academic history as a simple sequence, overlooking the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. This simplification can lead to inaccurate performance predictions, particularly for students with heavy or challenging course loads. This paper introduces a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation (TRACE) that addresses this limitation by jointly predicting both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester. Our approach encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture the effects of course concurrency and utilizes a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. We demonstrate that predicting courses taken in addition to the grades in those courses leads to significant improvements in prediction quality. Trained on ten years of institutional data, our joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture that predicts grades alone. The model also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models, as well as graph neural network-based approaches, and offers natural ways to incorporate student attribute data. This work demonstrates the utility of modern neural architectures for creating interpretable models that can be adapted to new institutions via retraining and recalibration, as well as the importance of key techniques, such as predicting courses taken during training. We discuss how this model could be incorporated into early detection systems at institutions of higher education.

AI.tldr: TRACE (TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation) is a novel model that jointly predicts both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for upcoming semesters, achieving 50% MAE reduction compared to grade-only prediction models.
AI.motivation: Existing predictive models in learning analytics treat student academic history as simple sequences, overlooking concurrent course-taking within semesters. This simplification leads to inaccurate performance predictions, especially for students with heavy or challenging course loads.
AI.method: TRACE encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture course concurrency effects and uses a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. It's based on Transformer architecture and incorporates student attribute data naturally.
AI.result: The joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to identical architecture predicting grades alone. It outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models and graph neural network approaches. Trained on ten years of institutional data.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the utility of modern neural architectures for creating interpretable models that can be adapted to new institutions via retraining/recalibration. The model could be incorporated into early detection systems at higher education institutions, highlighting the importance of predicting courses taken during training.

title: The Time Value of Evolution
comment: Submitted to AAAI 2026, 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables
summary: In evolutionary search, a weak child can be a valuable ancestor that makes high-fitness regions reachable. Immediate-return control is blind to this delayed utility, penalizing mutations through their immediate offspring even when they open productive future lineages. We formalize this hidden dynamic as the time value of evolution within a finite-horizon Markov decision process. To exploit it, we introduce Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic framework for automated trading policy discovery. Our architecture decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone: a bootstrapped critic head estimates the value of finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. We isolate the impact of long-horizon credit assignment against immediate-return optimization across 90 paired runs under matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets. Path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG also produces fewer temporary regressions than immediate-return optimization and recovers from them more often. Finite-horizon lineage value yields more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies within identical resource constraints.

AI.tldr: LVPG is a new evolutionary algorithm that uses long-horizon credit assignment to value mutations based on their descendants' potential, not just immediate offspring fitness, improving policy discovery efficiency.
AI.motivation: Traditional evolutionary search uses immediate-return control that penalizes mutations through their immediate offspring fitness, even when those mutations enable productive future lineages. This misses the "time value of evolution" where weak intermediate ancestors can be valuable for reaching high-fitness regions.
AI.method: Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG) - a long-horizon actor-critic framework with specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone. A bootstrapped critic estimates finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor dynamically modulates mutation intensity based on remaining search budget.
AI.result: In 90 paired runs with matched conditions, path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG produces fewer temporary regressions, recovers from them more often, and yields more selective non-monotonic search with stronger policies within identical resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: Finite-horizon lineage value provides superior credit assignment for evolutionary search, enabling more efficient policy discovery by valuing mutations based on their long-term lineage potential rather than just immediate fitness, making better use of limited search budgets.

title: Who Speaks Matters: Authority-Aware Multi-View RAG over Italian Parliamentary Proceedings
comment: Accepted at ISWC 2026 In-Use Track. Please cite the ISWC version
summary: Parliamentary proceedings are a primary record of democratic deliberation, yet their volume and fragmentation make multi-perspective access difficult for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to parliamentary transcripts introduces three specific risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers according to topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text. We present ParliamentRAG, a RAG system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that addresses these risks jointly. Its core contribution is a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the current query, combining interpretable components such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a user query, the system retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives, accompanied by supporting quotations. ParliamentRAG is evaluated against Google NotebookLM on 15 policy topics via a two-level protocol combining automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts. The system achieves higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.

AI.tldr: ParliamentRAG is a RAG system for Italian parliamentary transcripts that addresses biases by weighting speaker authority based on topical expertise and demographic factors, improving political coverage and citation faithfulness compared to NotebookLM.
AI.motivation: Parliamentary proceedings are voluminous and fragmented, making multi-perspective access difficult. Standard RAG systems introduce risks: dominance of frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers by topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive contexts.
AI.method: Developed ParliamentRAG with a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority based on profession, education, and previous interventions. For each query, it retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates summaries with supporting quotations.
AI.result: Evaluated against Google NotebookLM on 15 policy topics with automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts. Achieved higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions.
AI.conclusion: ParliamentRAG effectively addresses key risks in applying RAG to parliamentary transcripts through its topic-dependent authority modeling, improving political representation and citation accuracy while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose quality.

title: A Probe Direction Is a Property of Its Prompt
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 13 appendices. Code, data manifests and results: https://github.com/vcnoel/probe-direction
summary: A model that behaves differently when it senses it is being tested would undermine the evaluations we rely on, so recent work has sought to read that sense directly from a model's activations. The standard instrument contrasts activations on prompts that announce an evaluation against prompts that do not, and reports how well the resulting direction separates held-out cases. That number is then compared across models and correlated with scale. We observe that the instrument has a free parameter its readings do not disclose: "a prompt that announces an evaluation" is not a prompt but a choice among many, and nothing in the method fixes which. Holding the task text fixed and varying only that choice, we find that the reported score, and even the direction in which it trends with model size, follows the prompt rather than the model; two published studies that disagree about the sign of that trend are both reproducible from a single design, by choice of prompt alone. Treating the prompt as a facet of a measurement design rather than an implementation detail, we find the model under study accounts for a small share of the variance in the number reported about it, and most of the rest lies in how each model responds to each prompt: collecting more evaluation items cannot repair the measurement, while varying prompts can. A further check finds that the split these probes are scored on is largely separable from surface form alone, so a direction carrying no information about evaluation at all still reproduces a substantial fraction of each published score. We conclude that a single-prompt design cannot support comparison between models, and we give the number of prompts a defensible comparison requires.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques current activation probing methods for detecting evaluation awareness in LLMs, showing that single-prompt designs are unreliable for model comparisons as results heavily depend on prompt choice rather than actual model behavior.
AI.motivation: Recent work attempts to detect whether LLMs behave differently during evaluation by analyzing activations, but current methods are unreliable as they don't account for the substantial influence of prompt choice on results, leading to potentially misleading conclusions about model comparison and scaling trends.
AI.method: Analyzes the standard evaluation-awareness probing method, varying only the prompt that announces evaluation while keeping task text fixed. Conducts systematic experiments showing how prompt choice affects reported scores and scaling trends, measures variance attribution, and tests separability of probe directions from surface features.
AI.result: Evaluation awareness scores are highly sensitive to prompt choice rather than model characteristics; prompt variation explains most variance, model characteristics contribute little, and surface features alone can achieve substantial scores. Published conflicting trends can be reproduced from a single model by changing only the prompt.
AI.conclusion: Single-prompt designs cannot support reliable model comparisons for evaluation awareness; defensible comparisons require multiple prompts, and current methods need revision to properly attribute variance between model behavior and measurement design artifacts.

title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of improving models, systems, and other technical artifacts through long-horizon experimentation. To understand the current state of this capability, however, evaluation must go beyond final scores, which neither reveal where progress is gained or lost nor indicate whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. We therefore present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks based on a new framework that uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control and controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse within and across tasks. The results show that current agents operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but their performance varies substantially across runs, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty remains rare. Detailed analysis reveals that observed performance is shaped by multiple factors, including distinct process bottlenecks behind similar final outcomes, experience reuse that can help or mislead subsequent decisions, and harness designs that affect performance stability. These findings suggest concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic evaluation framework for autonomous agents on long-horizon tasks, revealing they function more as engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers with limited genuine novelty.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of autonomous agents focuses too much on final scores, which don't reveal where progress is gained/lost or whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. There's a need for systematic evaluation that characterizes within-run behavior and assesses experience reuse.
AI.method: Developed a new evaluation framework with rule-based metrics to characterize behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control. Conducted controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse within and across tasks, evaluating seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks.
AI.result: Current agents operate like engineering optimizers rather than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but performance varies substantially across runs, strongest solutions mainly adapt/combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty is rare. Detailed analysis revealed multiple shaping factors including distinct process bottlenecks, experience reuse that can help or mislead, and harness design affecting stability.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design, highlighting the need for more sophisticated evaluation beyond final scores to advance autonomous agent capabilities.

title: Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research
summary: The replicability of papers is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, ensuring the reliability of existing results and providing a base for further experiments. The act of replication typically illuminates details that were previously underspecified, and thus requires similar hypothesis-driven exploration to open-ended research. In this work, we develop Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication. To provide reward signal, we introduce an auto-generated rubric-based judge that has low noise and agrees with human assessment of replication quality. We post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter "AI Scientist" agent that leverages coding agents as tools, surpassing the performance of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis of individual rollouts reveals that Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach. We believe that our results provide a stepping stone towards AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses.

AI.tldr: Faraday, a 27B-parameter AI Scientist agent trained on the Replica paper replication task space, outperforms top models like Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 in replication tasks using an auto-generated rubric-based evaluation system.
AI.motivation: Paper replication is fundamental to scientific knowledge but challenging due to underspecified details, requiring hypothesis-driven exploration similar to original research. The authors aim to develop AI agents capable of scientific paper replication as a stepping stone toward long-horizon scientific innovation.
AI.method: 1) Created Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication. 2) Developed an auto-generated rubric-based judge for reward signals that aligns with human assessment. 3) Post-trained Faraday, a 27B-parameter "AI Scientist" agent that uses coding agents as tools.
AI.result: Faraday surpasses Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis shows Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach compared to other models.
AI.conclusion: The Replica task space and Faraday agent represent significant progress toward AI agents capable of complex scientific paper replication without requiring specialized harnesses, advancing toward long-horizon scientific innovation capabilities.

title: Enhancing Virtual Agents through SLMs and Edge-Computing: An Exploratory Evaluation of Think and Memory Processes
summary: Embodied intelligent virtual agents are expected to operate as persistent, adaptive, and context-aware entities within complex virtual and Metaverse worlds. However, implementing cognitively capable agents in such environments is conceptually and technologically challenging. Among a range of blueprints and development approaches, the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) has been developed as an implementation-oriented framework for architecting components of perception, memory, reasoning, planning, and embodied action. Considering the recent advances in edge computing and generative AI language models, this paper explores the use of Small Language Models (SLMs) to support edge-based operation of selected CEAA components, focusing on "Think" and "Memory" as processes central to cognitive orchestration and persistence of virtual agents in interactive virtual worlds. An edge-based virtual agent gateway system was developed and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX using Qwen2.5 models of different sizes, exploring the system's capability to process service requests and handle memory-driven conversations. A series of simulation experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes to support the development of embodied agents whose cognitive "brain" can operate efficiently and contextually for interactive experiences in immersive virtual worlds.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using Small Language Models (SLMs) on edge devices to implement cognitive processes for embodied virtual agents in Metaverse environments, demonstrating a prototype system on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligent virtual agents need to operate as persistent, adaptive, and context-aware entities in complex virtual/Metaverse worlds, but implementing cognitively capable agents is challenging. Recent advances in edge computing and generative AI create opportunities for more efficient, contextual operation.
AI.method: Developed an edge-based virtual agent gateway system using SLMs (Qwen2.5 models of different sizes) on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. Focused on implementing "Think" and "Memory" processes from the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA). Conducted simulation experiments evaluating routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency.
AI.result: Demonstrated an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes. The system showed capability to process service requests and handle memory-driven conversations efficiently on edge devices, supporting development of embodied agents with cognitive "brains" that operate contextually for interactive experiences.
AI.conclusion: SLMs can effectively support edge-based operation of cognitive processes for virtual agents, enabling efficient and contextual operation in immersive virtual worlds. This approach addresses challenges in implementing cognitively capable agents for Metaverse environments while leveraging edge computing advantages.

title: Neural Quadratic Forms: A Unified Minimal Model for Sudden Learning and Scaling Laws
summary: Neural networks trained by gradient descent on a smooth cost function can nevertheless learn in steps: the cost holds on long plateaus and then drops abruptly. Meanwhile, training losses instead follow smooth power laws. Variants of both behaviors occur in architectures with very different microscopic structures, which is the signature of a few relevant collective variables.
